research.domain: Solutions and what people can do (individual, community and policy levers; carbon inequality; whether the world is on track; which policies have worked)

sources.name: Drawdown Explorer: solutions table and per-solution assessment spreadsheets
sources.publisher: Project Drawdown
sources.measures: More than 100 climate solutions, each with a classification (Highly Recommended, Worthwhile, Keep Watching, Not Recommended, Coming Soon), sector, adoption unit, effectiveness (t CO2-eq (100-yr) per unit), current adoption, achievable adoption range, GHG impact (Gt CO2-eq (100-yr)/yr, low to high), cost (US$2023 per t CO2-eq), speed of action (Emergency Brake, Gradual, Delayed), pollutants, and co-benefits.
sources.coverage: Global, by solution. Achievable potential relative to a 2023 baseline. 165 rows in the CSV export: 58 Highly Recommended, 16 Worthwhile, 29 Keep Watching, 14 Not Recommended, 48 Coming Soon.
sources.latest_release: Explorer launched September 2025 and is updated continuously. Methodology v3 was published on Zenodo on 2025-12-23. CSV export Last-Modified was 2026-10-02. Solution pages show their own dates, e.g. Mobilize Electric Cars 'Last updated September 8, 2026'. Per-solution spreadsheets were published on Zenodo through 2026, e.g. Improve Diets and Use Heat Pumps on 2026-07-07.
sources.update_cadence: Rolling. Solutions are added and revised continuously, and the FAQ says all remaining solutions are expected during 2026.
sources.format: CSV (UTF-8 with BOM; values use Unicode superscripts such as 1.4×10⁷ and ranges like '0.05 to 0.12', so a parser is needed). Per-solution XLSX on Zenodo. Methodology PDF.
sources.license: Explorer FAQ (https://drawdown.org/explorer/faqs): 'Please use our materials – the numbers, the graphics, the maps, the analysis – in your work.' and 'We only ask that you give credit to Project Drawdown, link to the appropriate page(s), and cite our work'. The per-solution assessment spreadsheets and the methodology on Zenodo are CC BY 4.0: all 25 sampled records in the pdexplorer community were cc-by-4.0, and the community has 39 records. Caveat: the generic site Terms of Use (https://drawdown.org/terms-of-use) contain restrictive boilerplate ('you won't use, copy, reproduce ... any Content not owned by you ... without the prior consent of the owner'). Build from the CC BY Zenodo spreadsheets to avoid that ambiguity.
sources.citation: Project Drawdown. (Year, Month Date). The Drawdown Explorer. http://drawdown.org/explorer. For methods: Project Drawdown et al. (2025). Methodology for Project Drawdown Solutions Assessments (v3). Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18037237. Per-solution example: 'Improve Diets- Solution Assessment Spreadsheet', Zenodo, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21246101.
sources.doi: 10.5281/zenodo.18037237 (methodology). Per-solution DOIs, e.g. 10.5281/zenodo.21246101 (Improve Diets) and 10.5281/zenodo.21246268 (Use Heat Pumps).
sources.status: Active and expanding (48 of 165 rows are still 'Coming Soon'). It is a non-profit and not exposed to US federal cuts.
sources.url_check: The FAQ page loaded and confirmed the September 2025 launch, 'over 100 solutions', the data-reuse wording and the citation format. The explorer page HTML links to /explorer-solutions-table-export.csv and to zenodo.org/records/18037237. The CSV returned HTTP 200 text/csv (34,720 bytes, Last-Modified 2026-10-02). Header: Action, Solution, Solution Classification, Mode, Sector, Cluster, Adoption Unit, Effectiveness..., Adoption Current, Adoption Achievable Range, GHG Impact Gt CO₂-eq (100-yr)/yr, Cost US$ per t CO₂-eq, ... Top rows by upper GHG impact: Utility-Scale Solar PV 9.20 to 11.00 Gt/yr; Onshore Wind 5.40 to 7.50; Diets 1.40 to 2.80 (cost -8.54 $/t); Food Loss & Waste 1.23 to 2.47; Electric Cars 1.26 to 2.30 (-1019 $/t). The Zenodo API for record 18037237 returned v3, 2025-12-23, cc-by-4.0. The Zenodo community pdexplorer API returned total 39 records, all cc-by-4.0 in the first 25. /explorer/mobilize-electric-cars returned 200, with a 'Methods and Supporting Data' section linking to the Zenodo community.
sources.site_use: Main 'what can be done at scale' view: a bubble or bar chart of solutions by GHG impact range against cost, filterable by sector and speed (Emergency Brake vs Gradual), linking each personal action to its system-scale solution (e.g. Diets, Electric Cars, Heat Pumps). Each solution card should link to its Zenodo spreadsheet DOI for traceability.
sources.caveats: Potentials are ranges and not strictly additive across solutions. Costs are relative to a 2023 baseline and some are hugely negative (e.g. Nonmotorized Transportation -1771 $/t). The CSV is regenerated as solutions change, so snapshot it with a hash and an access date. Do not compare it with the older 2017/2020 Drawdown 'Table of Solutions' numbers because the methodology changed.

sources.name: IPCC AR6 WGIII Summary for Policymakers (Figure SPM.6 demand-side potential, Figure SPM.7 mitigation options cost and potential in 2030) and Chapter 5 (demand-side mitigation)
sources.publisher: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, Working Group III (Cambridge University Press). Figure data archived by the IPCC Data Distribution Centre on MetadataWorks.
sources.measures: SPM.7: net GHG emission reduction potential in 2030 (GtCO2-eq/yr) of 43 mitigation options, split by cost band (USD/tCO2-eq, from below 0 to 200). SPM.6 and Ch5: demand-side (avoid-shift-improve) potential by end-use sector in 2050, in % against a baseline.
sources.coverage: Global, by sector and option. Target year 2030 (SPM.7) and 2050 (SPM.6). Assessment based on literature up to about 2021, with about 175 underlying sources for SPM.7.
sources.latest_release: AR6 WGIII was published in 2022 and is still the latest IPCC mitigation assessment. The AR7 WGIII report has not been published as of 2026-10. SPM.7 figure data was published 2022-05-13 (DataCite).
sources.update_cadence: IPCC assessment cycle of roughly 6 to 8 years.
download_urls: https://doi.org/10.48490/ayfg-tv12 (SPM.7 data; currently resolves to a 404)
sources.format: PDF (report). The figure data is described as an Excel workbook but was not retrievable.
sources.license: Report text and figures follow IPCC copyright (https://www.ipcc.ch/copyright/): 'You may freely download and copy the material ... for your personal, non-commercial use, without any right to resell or redistribute it or to compile or create derivative works', and 'figures cannot be altered in any way'. For any other use 'permission is required'. The figure data: a web snippet claimed CC BY 4.0, but the DataCite record for 10.48490/ayfg-tv12 has an empty rightsList, so the license is unverified.
sources.citation: IPCC, 2022: Summary for Policymakers. In: Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change. Contribution of Working Group III to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change [P.R. Shukla, J. Skea, R. Slade, A. Al Khourdajie, R. van Diemen, D. McCollum, M. Pathak, S. Some, P. Vyas, R. Fradera, M. Belkacemi, A. Hasija, G. Lisboa, S. Luz, J. Malley (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, UK and New York, NY, USA. doi:10.1017/9781009157926.001. Data: Babiker, M.; Sugiyama, M.; Cohen, B.; Toribio Ramirez, D.; Blok, K. (2022). Data for Figure SPM.7 - Summary for Policymakers of the Working Group III Contribution to the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report. MetadataWorks. doi:10.48490/ayfg-tv12.
sources.status: The report is active (the PDFs return 200). The figure-data archive is at risk or broken. The DOI 10.48490/ayfg-tv12 redirects to ipcc-browser.ipcc-data.org/browser/dataset?id=447, which returns HTTP 404. ipcc-data.org returns 503. The former NASA SEDAC IPCC-DDC host (sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu) did not connect. The Columbia mirror serves a Cloudflare bot challenge.
sources.url_check: ipcc.ch figure pages returned 403 to WebFetch. With curl, the SPM.7 page HTML links to ipcc-browser.ipcc-data.org/browser/dataset?id=447, which returns 404. IPCC_AR6_WGIII_SummaryForPolicymakers.pdf returned 200 application/pdf (1.30 MB). Chapter05.pdf returned 200 (5.66 MB). Extracted SPM text: C.12 'Mitigation options costing USD100 tCO2-eq–1 or less could reduce global GHG emissions by at least half the 2019 level by 2030' and C.12.1 '(options costing less than USD20 tCO2-eq–1 are estimated to make up more than half of this potential)'. C.10: demand-side measures 'can reduce global GHG emissions in end-use sectors by 40–70% by 2050 compared to baseline scenarios'. DataCite API for 10.48490/ayfg-tv12 lists creators Babiker, Sugiyama, Cohen, Toribio Ramirez, Blok, publisher MetadataWorks, 2022, rightsList [], url pointing to the 404 page. The IPCC copyright page text was quoted directly.
sources.site_use: Authoritative framing statements, e.g. 'Options under $100/t could halve emissions by 2030' and 'Demand-side change could cut end-use emissions 40–70% by 2050'. Redraw SPM.7 as an original chart from the numbers, not a copy of the IPCC graphic, once the data workbook is recovered. Until then, show quoted SPM statements with page and paragraph references (C.10, C.12).
sources.caveats: Do not reproduce IPCC figures as images (no alteration permitted, non-commercial only, and permission needed for other uses). Restating facts and numbers with citation is fine. The SPM.7 potentials are not additive across options. The data is about 4 years old. Try to recover the SPM.7 workbook manually (e.g. via a human browser on the Columbia mirror, or by contacting the IPCC WGIII TSU) before relying on it.

sources.name: Ivanova et al. 2020: Quantifying the potential for climate change mitigation of consumption options (ERL systematic review)
sources.publisher: IOP Publishing / Environmental Research Letters (authors at Leeds, MCC Berlin, BOKU, SEI)
sources.measures: Mean (and range) GHG mitigation potential of 61 household consumption options in tCO2eq per capita per year, synthesised from 53 studies (about 7,000 data points). Covers mobility, housing/energy and food. Also reports average footprints (about 6 tCO2eq/cap global, 13.4 North America, 7.5 Europe, 1.7 Africa and Middle East).
sources.coverage: Mainly high-income countries (literature up to about 2019). Per-capita, annual.
sources.latest_release: Published 2020 (ERL 15, 093001). No updated edition.
sources.format: PDF (article). XLSX supplementary spreadsheet on IOP.
sources.license: CC BY 4.0. The article states: 'Original content from this work may be used under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license. Any further distribution of this work must maintain attribution to the author(s) and the title of the work, journal citation and DOI.' The Zenodo copy (record 4106717) is also cc-by-4.0.
sources.citation: Ivanova, D., Barrett, J., Wiedenhofer, D., Macura, B., Callaghan, M., & Creutzig, F. (2020). Quantifying the potential for climate change mitigation of consumption options. Environmental Research Letters, 15(9), 093001. https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/ab8589
sources.url_check: WebFetch of the IOP article page succeeded. It gave the license text and the top options, with means in tCO2eq/cap/yr: living car-free 2.0; battery electric vehicle 2.0; one less long-haul flight 1.9; renewable electricity 1.5; refurbishment/renovation 0.9; vegan diet 0.9; heat pump 0.8; renewable-based heating 0.7; one less medium-haul flight 0.6; improved cooking equipment 0.6. Curl to IOP returned a 'Radware Bot Manager Captcha' page, so the supplementary xlsx URL could not be retrieved. The Zenodo API for record 4106717 returned 200 with cc-by-4.0 and a 2.0 MB PDF.
sources.site_use: Core 'What can I do?' ranking: a horizontal bar chart of mean potential with min–max whiskers, colour-coded by domain (mobility, home, food). Each bar links to the matching Drawdown solution and to the calculators (DESNZ flights, Poore food, Ember grid).
sources.caveats: These are literature means, not additive, and depend on context (grid mix, baseline car, diet). They mostly reflect high-income consumers. Transcribe values from the paper's table or figure, record the table and figure number, and get the supplementary xlsx manually.

sources.name: Wynes & Nicholas 2017: The climate mitigation gap (high-impact individual actions), with the 2018 comment and reply
sources.publisher: IOP Publishing / Environmental Research Letters
sources.measures: Annual emission reductions (tCO2e/yr) of individual lifestyle actions for high-income individuals, compared with what textbooks and government guidance recommend. Values: one fewer child 58.6; live car-free 2.4; avoid one transatlantic return flight 1.6; plant-based diet 0.8.
sources.coverage: Developed countries (data from 39 sources). Annual, per person.
sources.latest_release: Published 2017 (ERL 12, 074024). Comment and reply published in ERL 13 (2018).
sources.format: HTML/PDF article. Supplementary material at stacks.iop.org/ERL/12/074024/mmedia.
sources.license: CC BY 3.0: 'Original content from this work may be used under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 licence.'
sources.citation: Wynes, S., & Nicholas, K. A. (2017). The climate mitigation gap: education and government recommendations miss the most effective individual actions. Environmental Research Letters, 12(7), 074024. https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aa7541. Critique: van Basshuysen, P., & Brandstedt, E. (2018). Comment on 'The climate mitigation gap...'. ERL 13, 048001. https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aab213
sources.url_check: WebFetch of the IOP article page succeeded: CC BY 3.0 text and values 58.6, 2.4, 1.6 and 0.8 tCO2e/yr. The LSE eprints PDF of the critique returned 200 application/pdf. The critique's main point, confirmed in its abstract: the 'one fewer child' figure relies on multiple counting of descendants' emissions and assumes trajectories that never reach net zero.
sources.site_use: Secondary comparison with Ivanova. Most useful for the 'recommendations miss the big actions' story (e.g. recycling or bulbs versus car-free living). Show the critique next to it.
sources.caveats: Do not headline '58.6 t per child'. It uses the Murtaugh & Schlax descendant-legacy accounting, which is contested (multiple counting, no net-zero scenarios). The values are older than Ivanova's. Prefer Ivanova as the default ranking.

sources.name: SEI Emissions Inequality Dashboard (global consumption CO2 by income percentile)
sources.publisher: Stockholm Environment Institute (SEI), in partnership with Oxfam
sources.measures: Shares of global income, population and consumption-based CO2 emissions for each global income percentile, with finer slices of the top 1% (down to p99.999–p100). Also country-level shares and totals, Theil decomposition (between and within countries), and SSP/RCP scenario projections.
sources.coverage: Historical 1990–2023 (the API returned 2023 records). Built from national consumption emissions combined with income distributions. The About page says 117 countries; the API country totals sum to a population of 7.87 billion in 2023.
sources.latest_release: Historical series through 2023, using the 2023 methodology update ('Climate Equality' 2023 and later). The figures Oxfam used in its 2025 releases come from this SEI research.
sources.format: JSON REST (records arrays with string-typed numbers).
sources.license: About page: 'Stockholm Environment Institute (SEI) holds the copyright of the Emissions Inequality Dashboard. It is licensed under Creative Commons and you are free to copy and redistribute material derived from the platform by following the guidelines of the Creative Commons License: CC BY'.
sources.citation: Emily Ghosh, Anisha Nazareth, Guozhong Wang, Sivan Kartha, Eric Kemp-Benedict (2021). Emissions Inequality Dashboard. Stockholm Environment Institute (SEI). https://emissions-inequality.org
sources.status: Active. Risk: the API is served from a domain named 'sei-eqtrans-dev.net' ('dev'), which could change without notice. Snapshot the responses.
sources.url_check: emissions-inequality.org/api/ listed 10 endpoints. GET globalHistoricalDataByYear?startyear=2023&endyear=2023 returned 200 JSON with 127 percentile records (p0p1 ... p99.999p100), fields Year, PercentileLabel, IncomeShare, EmissionShare, PopulationShare, Elasticity. Sums for 2023: top 10% EmissionShare 0.4708, top 1% 0.1655, bottom 50% 0.0842. For 2019: top 10% 0.4882, top 1% 0.1674, bottom 50% 0.0807. countryTotals for 2022–2023 returned SumPopulation 7,874,803,317 and SumNatEmisions 36,098,021,418 for 2023.
sources.site_use: Carbon-inequality drilldown: a 'carbon staircase' (emissions share against population share by global income percentile), a toggle for year 1990–2023, and a click into top 10%, top 1% and top 0.1%. Supports the message that both systemic policy and high-emitter lifestyle change matter.
sources.caveats: These are consumption-based CO2 only (not all GHGs). The figures depend on an income–emissions elasticity assumption and an emissions ceiling (Oxfam 2025 raised the ceiling from 300 to 3,000 tCO2/cap). Dashboard numbers differ from Oxfam's printed ones (e.g. top 1% in 2019 is 16.7% here versus 15.9% in Oxfam's Jan 2025 release), so always state the access date.

sources.name: Oxfam/SEI 'Climate Equality: A planet for the 99%' (2023) and Oxfam 2025 carbon-inequality releases
sources.publisher: Oxfam International (analysis by SEI)
sources.measures: Narrative report and datasets on emissions by income group (e.g. richest 1% = 16% of 2019 consumption emissions), billionaire and investment emissions, and heat-related deaths attributed to the emissions of the rich.
sources.coverage: Global, 1990–2019 (2023 report). 2025 releases ('Carbon Inequality Kills', Jan 2025; 'Climate Plunder', Oct 2025).
sources.latest_release: Climate Equality published 2023-11-20 (DOI 10.21201/2023.000001), with 'Dataset one' (113 KB) and 'Dataset two' (61 MB). The Oxfam press release of 2025-01-10 gives the top 1% at 15.9% of 2019 CO2 and 76 t/yr per capita, against 0.7 t/yr for the poorest 50%.
sources.format: PDF report, methodology note, XLSX datasets.
sources.license: Oxfam copyright & permissions: use for advocacy, education and research with attribution is allowed, but 'If you wish to make commercial use of any of our material, or if you wish to make any alterations or modifications (including translations), you must contact us for permission.' The DSpace record has no rights metadata.
sources.citation: Khalfan, A., Nilsson Lewis, A., Aguilar, C., Lawson, M., Jayoussi, S., Persson, J., Dabi, N., Acharya, S. (2023). Climate Equality: A planet for the 99%. Oxford: Oxfam International. https://doi.org/10.21201/2023.000001
sources.url_check: The policy-practice.oxfam.org page returned 200. It lists the date 20/11/2023, the authors, the DOI, and the documents (English paper 9 MB, methodology note 609 KB, Dataset one 113 KB, Dataset two 61 MB) with oxfamilibrary bitstream links. The DSpace API pid/find returned dc.date.issued 2023-11-20 and the DOI, but no rights field. The copyright page text was quoted. WebFetch of the Oxfam press release (2025-01-10) gave: top 1% share of 2019 = 15.9%, 76 t/yr; poorest 50% = 0.7 t/yr; per-capita 1.5°C budget 2.1 t.
sources.site_use: Cite only for context and link out. Do not redistribute Oxfam's datasets or modified figures. Use the SEI dashboard (CC BY) for the numbers instead.
sources.caveats: Advocacy publication. The no-modification clause conflicts with offering derived CSVs. Its numbers differ from current SEI dashboard values because the methodology was updated.

sources.name: World Inequality Lab: Chancel (2022) 'Global carbon inequality over 1990–2019' (WID.world carbon series)
sources.publisher: World Inequality Lab (Paris School of Economics). Paper in Nature Sustainability.
sources.measures: Per-capita GHG footprints (consumption plus wealth/investment-based) by global and national income group. 2019: bottom 50% about 1.6 t (12% of total), middle 40% 6.6 t (40.4%), top 10% 31 t (47.6%), top 1% about 17%. In 2019, 63% of individual-emission inequality was within countries.
sources.coverage: Global and national, 1990–2019.
sources.latest_release: Nature Sustainability 5, 931–938 (2022). Replication 'Codes & Data' are on Dropbox via lucaschancel.com. WID.world updates its carbon series periodically, but the latest vintage could not be verified because the wid.world pages return JS-only shells to automated fetch.
sources.update_cadence: Irregular (World Inequality Report editions; WID.world updates).
sources.format: ZIP (Stata code and data), XLSX figure data, PDF.
sources.license: Unverified. The Nature Sustainability article is not under a CC license (no licence field on nature.com). The Dropbox replication files carry no license. WID.world's terms page returned an empty or JS-only body, so its data license could not be confirmed.
sources.citation: Chancel, L. (2022). Global carbon inequality over 1990–2019. Nature Sustainability, 5, 931–938. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41893-022-00955-z
sources.status: Active, but the data is on personal Dropbox, which is fragile hosting.
sources.url_check: nature.com article page returned 200. Data availability: 'available at https://lucaschancel.com/global-carbon-inequality-1990-2019/ and on request'. No CC licence field found. lucaschancel.com returned 200 with four Dropbox links (codes & data zip, figures xlsx, SI pdf, main pdf). wid.world/terms-of-use, /world/ and /data/ returned tiny JS shells (114 bytes), so the license could not be read. wir2026.wid.world and wir2022.wid.world did not connect.
sources.site_use: Methodological cross-check for the SEI dashboard, and a quote for 'inequality within countries now dominates'. Do not offer as CSV until the license is confirmed with WIL.
sources.caveats: Includes investment-based emissions, which SEI does not, so its numbers are not interchangeable with SEI's. License is unclear.

sources.name: Global Carbon Budget 2025: national fossil CO2 emissions, territorial and consumption-based (with the Our World in Data processed version)
sources.publisher: Global Carbon Project (ICOS Carbon Portal). Derived charts by Our World in Data.
sources.measures: National territorial and consumption-based (trade-adjusted) fossil CO2 emissions (MtC, converted to MtCO2 by ×3.664), and per-capita values.
sources.coverage: About 220 countries and regional aggregates. Consumption-based 1990–2023 for countries; the OWID World series runs to 2024.
sources.latest_release: GCB 2025 (v15). ICOS object National_Fossil_Carbon_Emissions_2025_v1.0.xlsx (DOI 10.18160/GCP-2025). The GCB 2025 paper is in ESSD 18, 3211 (2026), Zenodo 22748763. OWID last updated 2025-11-13, with the next update expected 2026-11-13 (GCB 2026).
sources.format: XLSX (ICOS; download needs a click-through licence acceptance, no account). CSV (Zenodo territorial flat files; OWID).
sources.license: ICOS metadata for all three GCB 2025 objects: 'ICOS CCBY4 Data Licence' (CC BY 4.0). Zenodo record 17417124 (fossil CO2 2025v15) is cc-by-4.0. OWID's indicator metadata lists origin license 'CC BY 4.0' (https://www.icos-cp.eu/data-services/about-data-portal/data-license).
sources.citation: Friedlingstein, P. et al. (2026). Global Carbon Budget 2025. Earth System Science Data, 18, 3211. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-3211-2026. Data: Global Carbon Project (2025). National Fossil Carbon Emissions 2025 v1.0, ICOS. https://doi.org/10.18160/GCP-2025. If using OWID: 'Global Carbon Budget (2025); Population based on various sources (2024) – with major processing by Our World in Data'. Territorial flat files: Andrew, R. M., & Peters, G. P. (2025). The Global Carbon Project's fossil CO2 emissions dataset (2025v15). Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17417124
sources.status: Active. Not a US federal product. Next release expected around November 2026.
sources.url_check: doi.org/10.18160/GCP-2025 redirected to icos-cp.eu/impact/science/global-carbon-budget/2025 (200), which links three ICOS objects. The meta.icos-cp.eu JSON returned fileName National_Fossil_Carbon_Emissions_2025_v1.0.xlsx (755,198 bytes), doi 10.18160/GCP-2025, licence 'ICOS CCBY4 Data Licence'. The Zenodo API for 17417124 returned v15 (2025-10-22, cc-by-4.0) with GCB2025v15_MtCO2_flat.csv and percapita/population files. The OWID CSV returned columns entity, code, year, consumption_emissions_per_capita. Latest values: World 2024 4.73 t; United States 2023 15.81; China 2023 7.63; EU-27 2023 7.33; UK 2023 7.09; India 2023 1.77; Africa 2023 0.99; high-income 2023 11.09; low-income 2023 0.09. OWID metadata: lastUpdated 2025-11-13, nextUpdate 2026-11-13.
sources.site_use: The 'my country's footprint' entry point: a map and ranking of consumption-based per-capita CO2, a toggle between territorial and consumption-based, and a compare-to-world-average marker. It feeds the 'what can I do' page by showing where a visitor starts.
sources.caveats: OWID's processing changes values. OWID converts C to CO2 with ×3.664 (which GCB also recommends) but divides by OWID's own population series, not GCB's, so per-capita values can differ slightly from GCB's percapita files. Consumption data lags territorial data by one year. Fossil CO2 only (no land use, no non-CO2). Store the exact ICOS file hash.

sources.name: Poore & Nemecek (2018) food life-cycle emissions (via the Our World in Data processed series)

sources.coverage: Global meta-analysis of about 38,700 farms and 1,600 processors in 119 countries. Reference year 2010.
sources.latest_release: Science 2018. ORA dataset deposit 'LCA Meta-Analysis of Food Products - Full Model v0' (DOI 10.5287/bodleian:0z9MYbMyZ). OWID indicator lastUpdated 2019-10-08.
sources.format: CSV (OWID). XLSX full model (17.4 MB) on ORA.
sources.license: OWID publishes its charts and data under CC BY 4.0, but third-party data remains subject to the original terms. The ORA deposit shows 'Licence: Terms and Conditions of Use for Oxford University Research Archive' (not CC). The Science article is paywalled.
sources.citation: Poore, J., & Nemecek, T. (2018). Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers. Science, 360(6392), 987–992. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaq0216. Data via 'Poore and Nemecek (2018) – processed by Our World in Data'. Dataset: Poore, J. (2018). LCA Meta-Analysis of Food Products. University of Oxford. https://doi.org/10.5287/bodleian:0z9MYbMyZ
sources.url_check: The OWID ghg-per-kg-poore CSV returned 200: beef (beef herd) 99.48, dark chocolate 46.65, lamb & mutton 39.72, beef (dairy herd) 33.3, coffee 28.53 kgCO2eq/kg; potatoes 0.46, apples 0.43. Metadata: unit kgCO2eq per kilogram, lastUpdated 2019-10-08, citation 'Poore and Nemecek (2018) – processed by Our World in Data'. The ghg-per-protein-poore CSV returned (per 100 g protein): beef herd 49.89, lamb 19.85, cheese 10.82, pig 7.61, poultry 5.70, eggs 4.21, tofu 1.975, other pulses 0.836, peas 0.441, nuts 0.263. The ORA page returned 200, showing DOI 10.5287/bodleian:0z9MYbMyZ, the full-model xlsx (17.4 MB), and the ORA Terms licence.
sources.site_use: Food drilldown: ranked bars per 100 g protein and per kg, a 'swap' explorer (beef to beans, dairy milk to soy), and links to Drawdown 'Improve Diets' (1.4–2.8 Gt/yr) and Ivanova 'vegan diet 0.9 t/cap/yr'.

Before offering CSV downloads, confirm reuse with OWID and the Oxford authors, or offer only a link to OWID's download rather than re-hosting.

sources.name: UK Government GHG Conversion Factors for Company Reporting 2026 (DESNZ), for flight, home-energy and travel calculators. US EPA equivalents noted.
sources.publisher: UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) / DEFRA. For comparison: US EPA GHG Emission Factors Hub and eGRID.

OGL allows commercial and non-commercial reuse and adaptation with attribution ('Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0').

GOV.UK. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/greenhouse-gas-reporting-conversion-factors-2026. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

sources.url_check: GOV.UK content API (collection) returned 200, listing 'Greenhouse gas reporting: conversion factors 2026' (public_updated_at 2026-07-31). The publication API listed 4 attachments with asset URLs and sizes (full set 2.11 MB, flat file 515 KB, methodology 1.76 MB). The flat xlsx parsed. Its front page says 'Version: 1.2 ... Next publication date: 2027-06-01'. Row 21_316_3170_11_1 (Long-haul, to/from UK, Economy class, With RF): 0.11704 kg CO2e/passenger.km. Row 21_316_3171_11_1 (Without RF): 0.06926. Domestic average With RF: 0.22928. The methodology PDF says the published factors already include the 8% great-circle uplift and the RF uplift ('The figures in Table 38 DO NOT include the 8% uplift for Great Circle distance NOR the uplift ... which are applied to the conversion factors provided in the 2026 GHG Conversion Factors set'). It recommends an RF multiplier of 1.7 (Lee et al. 2021). EPA hub page returned 200 and lists '2025 GHG Emission Factors Hub (xlsx) ... January 2025'. eGRID page returned 200 and references eGRID2023.
sources.site_use: Powers transparent calculators: 'your flight' (great-circle distance × factor, showing both the with-RF and without-RF values), 'your car' per km, and 'your gas boiler vs heat pump' per kWh, combined with Ember grid intensity for non-UK countries. sources.caveats: Factors are UK reporting averages and not universal. Do not add another 8% distance uplift (it is already included). WTT emissions are separate rows. The RF choice changes flight results by about 1.7×, so always show both. Calculators must use these documented factors directly, with no invented defaults.

We identified 63 successful policy interventions with total emission reductions between 0.6 billion and 1.8 billion metric tonnes CO2 ... important role of price-based instruments in well-designed policy mixes'. The Zenodo API for 12773811 returned v4, cc-by-4.0, and 40+ files (README.txt, CAPMF_Policy.csv 8.1 MB, Forward_causal_step_shift_numbers.csv with header ISO, Module, Unique_Years, ...). headline_numbers.statement: The richest 10% of people on Earth (by income) caused about 47% of consumption-based CO2 emissions in 2023, the richest 1% about 16.5%, and the poorest half about 8%.
headline_numbers.derivation: GET https://www.sei-eqtrans-dev.net/api/globalHistoricalDataByYear/search.php?startyear=2023&endyear=2023 returns 127 records. drilldown_paths: Where do I stand? → What moves the needle? Country consumption CO2 per capita (GCB 2025 via OWID, or ICOS xlsx) → where that sits in the global income distribution (SEI dashboard percentiles) → ranked personal actions with ranges (Ivanova 2020; Wynes & Nicholas shown with critique) → personal calculators (DESNZ 2026 flight and energy factors, Poore & Nemecek food, Ember grid intensity) → the system-scale version of the same action (Drawdown solution card with Gt/yr and $/t, linked to its Zenodo spreadsheet DOI).

Food: from plate to planet. Drawdown 'Improve Diets' (1.40–2.80 Gt CO2-eq/yr; cost -8.54 $/t) → product footprints per kg, per 100 g protein and per 1,000 kcal (Poore & Nemecek via OWID) → swap explorer (beef to beans) → Ivanova vegan or vegetarian diet potential (0.9 t/cap/yr) → IPCC SPM C.10 demand-side 40–70% context.

Transport: is an EV really better where I live? ICCT 2025 EU lifecycle (63 vs 235 g/km) → Knobloch 2020 (53 of 59 regions already better) → Ember 2025 grid CO2 intensity for the visitor's country → Ivanova car-free (2.0) and BEV (2.0) → flights calculator (DESNZ factors with and without RF) → Drawdown 'Mobilize Electric Cars' and 'Nonmotorized Transportation'.

Home energy: heat pumps and clean power. Ivanova heat pump (0.8) and renewable electricity (1.5) → Ember grid intensity and trend → Drawdown 'Use Heat Pumps' spreadsheet (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.21246268) and 'Distributed Solar PV' → DESNZ kWh factors for a gas-boiler vs heat-pump comparison with every assumption shown.

The solutions menu (system level). IPCC AR6 SPM C.12 (≤$100/t options can halve 2019 emissions by 2030) → Drawdown Explorer table: filter by sector, speed (Emergency Brake) and classification → solution detail (adoption now vs achievable, Gt/yr range, $/t, co-benefits) → source spreadsheet DOI. The IPCC SPM.7 bar chart is redrawn only once its data workbook is recovered.

Is the world on track? UNEP EGR 2025 global gap (current policies 2.8°C; 35% and 55% cuts needed by 2035) ↔ CAT thermometer (2.6°C policies; 2.2°C pledges) → country: CAT rating, then the Climate Watch 2025 NDC card (2035 target? strengthened? net-zero status? link to the UNFCCC PDF), then OECD CAPMF policy stringency, then the World Bank carbon-pricing coverage of that jurisdiction, then links out to Climate Change Laws of the World.

What actually worked (evidence for citizens and policymakers). Stechemesser 2024: 63 successful interventions out of about 1,500, filterable by country and sector → policy mixes vs single instruments (pricing in mixes) → World Bank: nearly 30% of global emissions priced, 87 instruments, $107 bn revenue (2025) → the visitor's country CAPMF stringency trend.

Fairness and responsibility. SEI percentile 'carbon staircase' 1990–2023 (top 10%, 1%, 0.1%) → between-country vs within-country inequality (SEI Theil API; Chancel 2022 as a cross-check) → country consumption vs territorial emissions (GCB) → what high emitters can change most (flights, cars, investments), linked back to the action ranking.

You are not alone (civic action). Andre et al. 2024: actual support (69%, 86%, 89%) vs perceived support by country → why talking about it matters (pluralistic ignorance) → the policies that worked (Stechemesser) → your country's pledge and rating (Climate Watch, CAT) → link out to the official NDC and law texts so visitors can cite them to representatives.
research.action_links:
Individual. Rank actions by evidence, not by intuition. Ivanova et al. 2020 (CC BY 4.0, doi:10.1088/1748-9326/ab8589) puts car-free living (2.0 t/yr), switching to an EV (2.0), skipping long-haul flights (1.9 per flight avoided), renewable electricity (1.5), a vegan diet (0.9) and heat pumps (0.8) at the top, well above recycling or light bulbs (Wynes & Nicholas 2017, CC BY 3.0, used with its critique). Personal calculators should use documented factors only. For flights and energy use DESNZ 2026 (OGL v3.0), showing factor IDs; for food, Poore & Nemecek via OWID; for country grid intensity when judging EVs and heat pumps, Ember 2025 (CC BY 4.0). Every number must be shown with its source and vintage.

High emitters. The SEI dashboard (CC BY) shows the top 10% caused about 47% of consumption CO2 in 2023. Actions by the affluent (flying, car ownership, home energy, and where they invest) carry outsized weight, so the site should show visitors where they sit on the global distribution.

Community. Andre et al. 2024 (Nature Climate Change, CC BY 4.0) finds 69% of people would give 1% of income and 89% want more government action, yet people underestimate each other. Talking openly about climate action is a concrete, evidence-based lever. Drawdown solution pages (credit and link required; the spreadsheets are CC BY 4.0) give local-scale options such as distributed solar, heat pumps, food waste, and walking or cycling.

Policymakers and civic asks. Stechemesser et al. 2024 (Science; data CC BY 4.0) shows that well-designed policy mixes including carbon pricing produced the large emission cuts. The World Bank 2026 report (CC BY 3.0 IGO) shows pricing covers nearly 30% of emissions with over $107 bn of revenue in 2025. IPCC AR6 WGIII SPM C.12 says options at ≤$100/t could halve 2019 emissions by 2030, and C.10 says demand-side measures could cut end-use emissions 40–70% by 2050. Country accountability: CAT ratings and thermometer (non-commercial, credit plus copyright notice), Climate Watch NDC 3.0 content (CC BY 4.0, linking the UNFCCC NDC PDF), the UNEP EGR 2025 gap (35% and 55% cuts needed by 2035), and OECD CAPMF stringency. These let a visitor turn 'what can I do?' into a specific, cited request to their representative, e.g. 'our 2035 NDC target is X; CAT rates our policies Y; policy mixes with pricing are what worked elsewhere (Stechemesser 2024)'.
research.gaps_and_risks:
1. Bot protection on primary hosts blocks automated verification and scheduled fetching. UNEP (unep.org, wedocs) serves a Cloudflare challenge and 403. UNFCCC (NDC Registry) returns an Incapsula 'Request unsuccessful' page. The World Bank Carbon Pricing Dashboard serves a Cloudflare challenge, and datacatalogapi returned 429. The IPCC DDC Columbia mirror serves a Cloudflare challenge. IOP (supplementary files) serves a Radware captcha. The OECD terms page and IEA reports returned 403. In those cases I used fallback routes rather than the publisher pages: Crossref and DataCite metadata, the DSpace REST APIs at the World Bank and Oxfam, Europe PMC abstracts, and Zenodo. The ingest pipeline should be a manual or semi-manual monthly snapshot (download by a human, SHA-256 hash, archive to the repo or R2 with the access date). It should not be a Cloudflare Worker cron hitting these hosts, which also keeps cost under $20/month.

2. The IPCC AR6 WGIII figure data is at risk. The SPM.7 data DOI (10.48490/ayfg-tv12) resolves to a 404 on the IPCC MetadataWorks browser. ipcc-data.org returns 503, and the old NASA SEDAC IPCC-DDC host does not connect. The DataCite rightsList is empty, so the data license is unconfirmed. The report PDFs are fine. IPCC figure images cannot be altered or reused beyond personal non-commercial use without permission, so redraw from the numbers.

3. License conflicts to respect in CSV downloads:
- Climate Action Tracker: non-commercial, credit, copyright notice required.
- Oxfam: non-commercial, no modifications without permission (avoid as a data source).
- ICCT: © with no open license (cite numbers only).
- Poore & Nemecek raw data: Oxford ORA Terms; OWID re-publishes it but third-party terms still apply.
- Global Climate Change Survey microdata: IIL-1.0, registration and non-commercial (use paper aggregates only).
- WID.world, Chancel data on Dropbox, and Climate Change Laws of the World: license unverified.
- Drawdown: the explorer FAQ permits reuse with credit, but the generic site ToS is restrictive, so build from the CC BY 4.0 Zenodo spreadsheets.

The site should store a per-dataset license field and stamp each CSV with source, license, DOI and access date.

4. Version and methodology drift:
- SEI dashboard values differ from Oxfam's printed figures (2019 top 1%: 16.7% from the API vs 15.9% in Oxfam's January 2025 release), and its API lives on a domain named 'sei-eqtrans-dev.net'.
- The Drawdown CSV is regenerated continuously (48 of 165 rows 'Coming Soon'; Last-Modified 2026-10-02).
- OWID per-capita values use OWID's population series, not GCB's.
- Ember CO2 intensity appears to be lifecycle-based and should not be mixed with DESNZ direct factors.
- DESNZ factors already include the 8% great-circle uplift; do not double-apply it.

5. Contested numbers. Wynes & Nicholas' 'one fewer child = 58.6 t/yr' is disputed (van Basshuysen & Brandstedt 2018, ERL 13 048001) and should not be a headline. Ivanova potentials are literature means, not additive, and skewed to high-income contexts.

6. Staleness and US federal risk:
- EPA GHG Emission Factors Hub: latest edition '2025' (January 2025) with no 2026 edition on a page updated 2026-01-12.
- EPA eGRID: still eGRID2023 on a page updated 2026-09-21.
Treat both as at-risk and prefer DESNZ (OGL) plus Ember (CC BY). AR6 dates from 2022 and AR7 WGIII is not yet out. UNEP EGR 2026 and GCB 2026 are both due around November 2026, so update the headline numbers then.

7. Not verified this session (web search budget was exhausted mid-task):
- the UNEP EGR 2025 license and the 57.7 GtCO2e figure (taken from Carbon Brief);
- the World Bank dashboard data license;
- OECD's CC BY 4.0 data policy;
- CCLW terms;
- an official count of Parties with 2025 NDCs from UNFCCC. Climate Watch shows 151 'Submitted 2025 NDC' locations, counting the EU both as a bloc and as members, so do not publish that as a Party count.
No open-licensed heat-pump lifecycle dataset was found. The IEA 'Future of Heat Pumps' returned 403 and Knobloch 2020 is paywalled. Use Ivanova plus Drawdown 'Use Heat Pumps' (CC BY) and present a heat-pump calculator only with explicit DESNZ factors and stated efficiency inputs.

8. Process note: during verification one copy of the Drawdown CSV was saved to the session scratchpad (dd.csv). No project files were created or modified.

verdicts.corrections:

- BEV: 'average and median of 2.0'.
- One less long return flight: mean 1.9, median 1.7, range 0.7 to 4.5.
- Renewable electricity: mean 1.5, median 1.6.

1) Systems Change Lab and the State of Climate Action 2025 (WRI and Bezos Earth Fund, with Climate Action Tracker, ClimateWorks and others). This is the most authoritative sector-by-sector answer to 'is the world on track?'.
- Data: https://systemschangelab.org/ (Download Data at /download).
- Report: https://www.wri.org/research/state-climate-action-2025, DOI 10.46830/wrirpt.25.00006, published 2025-10-22, 137 pages. Its finding: 'None of the 45 indicators assessed are on track to reach their 1.5°C-aligned targets by the end of this decade'.

- Citation: 'Systems Change Lab. 2025. Washington, DC: World Resources Institute, Bezos Earth Fund'.
- Recommended priority: core.

2) Indicators of Global Climate Change (Forster, Smith et al.): the remaining carbon budget, human-induced warming and annual GHG totals.
- Latest data: 'Indicators of Global Climate Change 2025', Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.21494229, published 2026-07-22, cc-by-4.0 (VERIFIED). It is a supplement to github.com/ClimateIndicator/data at tag IGCC-2025a.
- Latest verified paper: IGCC 2024, ESSD 17, 2641, doi 10.5194/essd-17-2641-2025, 2025-06-19, CC BY 4.0. Check whether a 2026 ESSD paper accompanies the 2025 data.
- Recommended priority: core for 'how much budget is left'.

3) OWID co2-data on GitHub (https://github.com/owid/co2-data, CC BY 4.0; verify the current commit). It gives a git-versioned, hashable copy of the GCB-based series, which is more reproducible than grapher CSV endpoints.

4) Net Zero Tracker (Energy & Climate Intelligence Unit, Oxford Net Zero, NewClimate Institute, Data-Driven EnviroLab), https://zerotracker.net/. It covers net-zero targets for countries, regions, cities and companies, and has a 'Download Data' link. The licence was NOT visible on the homepage or the /terms page; verify it before reuse.

5) Climate TRACE (https://climatetrace.org/data): asset-level emissions for the 'who emits where' drill-down. The /data page says 'The data are licensed Creative Commons 4.0' (VERIFIED wording). Confirm which CC 4.0 variant from its data guide.

6) UNFCCC NDC Synthesis Report 2025 (FCCC/PA/CMA/2025/8, https://unfccc.int/ndc-synthesis-report). This is the official aggregate effect of the new NDCs on 2030/2035 emissions and is needed alongside UNEP and CAT. unfccc.int blocks automation (Incapsula), so download it by hand. Licence: UN copyright, verify.

7) EDGAR (EC JRC), https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/: all-GHG (CO2, CH4, N2O, F-gas) national totals. GCB covers fossil CO2 only, so EDGAR is needed for any 'total GHG by country' claim. Stated licence CC BY 4.0; verify.
